hn.title: Launch HN: Pomerado (YC F26) – Turn any website into an MCP for agents
hn.text:
Hi HN, we’re Alan and Akshay from Pomerado (https://pomerado.ai/). We connect your agents to any website by turning sites into deterministic, self-healing APIs in minutes, fully self-serve.
Agents are no longer limited by their intelligence, but rather by their ability to interact with systems. Airlines, banks, e-commerce, insurance portals, government sites, and legacy portals all lack APIs or MCPs and are common parts of personal assistant or business workflows. Agents instead rely on browser automation or computer use, which can be slow, expensive, and unreliable. And even if computer use were perfect, most companies have banned it out of security and compliance concerns.
We discovered this problem while tinkering with our own personal assistants. When OpenClaw came out, we wanted to “live our lives through our agents” and have them do everything for us. We soon found their usefulness was restricted by what tools they could connect to. For example, when trying to book flights, they fell back on computer use, which failed to checkout. These issues got magnified on repeated workflows, like searching many airlines at once.
Pomerado started off as a project to improve these personal assistant workflows. As we started building, we realized that just-in-time tool creation could have significant applications for AI builders in legacy verticals.
We’re ex-McKinsey and Scale AI, where we drove agent deployments in healthcare, professional services, and telecom. Each time, the biggest bottleneck was getting agents to interface well with legacy websites and apps.
Pomerado is what we built. It’s a self-serve platform where devs can create APIs for any website (even those they don’t own), in minutes. Users (or their coding agents) provide a short natural language description, answer a few questions about their workflow, and receive a MCP in less than an hour. Future tool calls use the deterministic MCP, which usually returns results in 5-30 seconds.
Here’s a walkthrough of our product: https://youtu.be/Bi4jci7rgHo
In practice:
- Our agent opens a browser, explores the website, and performs the requested task once by writing HTTP requests or a Playwright script. This example run establishes how to navigate the website, interact with the relevant controls, and obtain the desired result. If any additional user input is needed (e.g., login, clarification) the agent will ask the user over MCP.
- Afterwards, the agent uses the example run, along with all of the data it recorded, to create a generalizable and repeatable API. Throughout this process, a separate Guardian model reviews the coding agent’s calls against a set of guardrails. We also run a battery of tests with synthetic inputs to ensure that the API is generalized and not overfit to one input. A final publication agent ensures that the integration publishes a reasonable and generalized input/output schema
- We also handle sites that require authentication and 2FA. For authentication, we pass off to a deterministic sign-in process to ensure the model and our recorders never read customer credentials. Users can store 2FA TOTP seeds or link their account to a Pomerado phone number for us to autofill 2FA for them as well
- If future runs fail, a maintenance job is kicked off to repair and improve the tool. The maintenance job can fix broken steps (e.g., a renamed button), add additional functionality (e.g., searching for business class flights in addition to economy), or add new guardrails (e.g., reservation dates must be in the future). We’ve even seen people improve tools by just saying “please make this faster”
Unlike computer use, our MCPs are deterministic at runtime, which makes them much faster and cheaper. By taking slightly longer to do a task the first time, you reap the benefits much more in the future. It’s a great fit for repeated, high-volume tasks you want your agent to do.
We’d love to have you try it! We have both an open-source (MIT)…

Fixed an issue where plugin panels showed blank in pinned side panel tabs, covered the edges of the side panel, or stayed on screen over a maximized side panel.
Fixed an issue where a plugin's context providers were missing after you added it from its full-page details screen.
Fixed an issue where a plugin that declared extra fields in its manifest lost all of its context providers.
Fixed an issue where plugin panels could not play sound until you interacted with them.
Fixed an issue where conversation titles sometimes guessed what an abbreviation in your first message stood for instead of keeping it as written.

We are introducing the Gemini Decisions API to help you make fast, probabilistic choices across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. This tool computes confidence scores for multiple questions in a single pass, providing a cost-effective way to route queries, grade content, or check policy rules. You can start building today by accessing your API key in Google AI Studio and reviewing our documentation for Python, JavaScript, and REST guides.
Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.
Today, we’re introducing the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model (gemini-decision-1), available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio.
The Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. Rather than generating answer text token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores your candidate options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores in 150-250 ms end-to-end latency at $0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed.
Strong performance and calibration
On benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error.
Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API.
Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one pass
Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost.
You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer:
noul (Yes/No): Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria.
choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate.
score (Ordered Rubric): Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities.

article.title: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
article.text:
Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine
Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex
Ellie Huxtable
27 Oct 2026
— 4 min read
Share
Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine
Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex on another machine — with all context intact. Install, then run atuin resume
0:00
/0:13
Over the past year or two, how I use my terminal has changed dramatically. For years I was the sole user of my shell, and everything in my Atuin history was authored by me. Now, more than half the commands running on my machines weren’t written by me.
These days, much of my work happens through a coding agent, typed into a little “Topsy-turvying” text box. But while my shell history follows me everywhere, my agent sessions do not. They're scattered across different tools and machines (a laptop, a dev server, ephemeral instances on exe.dev, a surprisingly cheap bare metal box in Germany), difficult to search, and often forgotten once I've moved on.
It’s a familiar problem!
I started working on Atuin because the history of my work was ephemeral: every command I typed was destined to vanish on line 501 of .bash_history. But once this work became indexed, everlasting, and easy to recall, I could find the exact command I’d used to fix something years ago, in seconds.
Over the years, this data compounded. It became the history of all of my work, the record of how I solved problems and built things.
Shell history has always been an excellent record of what happened, but it’s only the surface. It never kept the reasoning… or the intentions behind what I was trying to do. I could only find a command if I remembered a part of it, though often I remembered what I was trying to achieve more readily.
Agent sessions store the lot of it. Every command, its output, my intent, and everything I tried along the way to the eventual solution. It’s all there, in plain English, in my home directory! But just as with shell history all those years ago, we don’t put it to work.
Atuin Threads
That is why we built Atuin Threads.
Starting with Atuin 18.24, you can search your agent sessions across machines, resume them anywhere, or fork the session into a different agent harness. Start something in Claude Code on a dev server, then finish it in Codex on your laptop.
Behind the scenes, this was a natural extension of Atuin. We put a lot of time and effort into building a reliable, encrypted sync engine. It’s generic, and can sync anything that can be modelled as an append-only log. As it turns out, most AI sessions are exactly this.
Like shell history, Threads is end-to-end encrypted when synced, so we can't read your sessions. You can use our hosted sync server, run your own, or keep everything local. Capturing agent sessions is opt-in, too.
Run atuin resume, and after setting up, you will see the TUI from the top of this post!
It doesn’t matter which agent you started with - you can resume it anywhere. With Atuin’s sync, this works across devices, and keeps your history backed up forever.
Right now, we support
Claude Code
Codex
Pi
Omp
OpenCode
with more agents coming soon.
MCP
With MCP, agents can search and reference previous sessions themselves. They can find work you’ve done before, understand why a decision was made, and build on previous investigations without having to dig up the context.
Our MCP is available as atuin mcp, and can be automatically installed with
atuin mcp install claude/codex/pi/opencode
There are all sorts of ways to put this history to work. A few examples:
Work that never shipped
I’ve iterated on our onboarding and setup so many times over the past few months, but never quite been happy with it. When I ask an agent to work on onboarding now, it finds all my previous attempts, as well as why they had been abandoned and what can be done better.

article.title: After 7-months, Glasswing Overwelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings | Blog | VulnCheck
article.text:
VulnCheck Community gives you free access to VulnCheck KEV, NVD++, Initial Access Community, and VulnCheck XDB
Join Now
Key Takeaways:
Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild.
Of Anthropic’s 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed.
Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes, widening the gap between discovery and remediation.
Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn.
Anthropic’s claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%, raising questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings.
Anthropic’s OSS Scanner shifts validation work to maintainers, with curl rejecting 19 of 34 published reports as vulnerabilities, confirming six as low severity and leaving nine awaiting assessment. Also putting Anthropic's true positive rates into question.
We're seven months into Anthropic's flagship Project Glasswing, and it's time for another update on the results. I've been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality.
As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, "We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers." What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign.
That said, we shouldn't overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model's capabilities.
If you're just catching up, this builds on my earlier posts:
Tracking CVEs Attributed to Anthropic Researchers and Project Glasswing - April 15
Observations on Anthropic's Vulnerability Disclosure Ledger - June 9
1H-2026 State of Exploitation Report - July 28
The Anthropic Glasswing Receipts Are Starting to Trickle In - September 8
So let's look at the results…
Tracking Anthropic-Discovered Vulnerabilities
I started tracking Anthropic's discovered vulnerabilities on April 17th, shortly after launch, in an open source repo called Anthropic Credited CVEs. The goal was to see whether Anthropic's claims lived up to the hype. This was before Anthropic launched its own disclosure ledger, which is only updated in infrequent bulk batches.
My repo tracks every vulnerability attributable to Anthropic using CVE records, GHSAs, Linux kernel commits, and Anthropic's own ledger. I also manually audit advisories to catch CVEs that might otherwise get overlooked.
After seven months, I've tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic. That's an average of just 63 per month. Out of the 93,450 CVEs published this year, that's only about 0.5% of all CVEs.
For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself.
The Danger Narrative Isn't Adding Up
You may recall that Glasswing launched with the message that we'd entered the Mythos era of vulnerability discovery. But are these vulnerabilities actually useful to attackers? To find out, I've been tracking Anthropic-discovered CVEs against VulnCheck KEV. So far, only 2 of the 442 have been exploited in the wild, just 0.45%. (CVE-2026-61500 and CVE-2026-26980)
Anthropic's Ledger Continues to Underwhelm
When Anthropic first launched its ledger in May, it reported 23,019 findings and a 90.8% true positive rate. As of its most recent update on November 2nd, there are 37,966 findings and just 217 fixes. That looks like a staggering failure to me, but let's take a closer look.

article.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers - CBS News
article.text:
MoneyWatch
United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
By
Megan Cerullo
Reporter, MoneyWatch
Megan Cerullo is a New York-based reporter for CBS MoneyWatch covering small business, workplace, health care, consumer spending and personal finance topics. She regularly appears on CBS News 24/7 to discuss her reporting.
Read Full Bio
Megan Cerullo
November 11, 2026 / 2:37 PM EST
/ MoneyWatch
Add CBS News on Google
United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing security risks and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.
Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.
To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."
The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances.
"As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.
United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group.
"United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."
Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app.
United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline."
"But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.

article.title: Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data | Claude by Anthropic
article.text:
Introducing Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data
Now you can brainstorm on whiteboards, build sheets, and share data directly in Claude.
CategoryProduct updates
ProductClaude apps
DateNovember 10, 2026
Reading time6 min
Share
Today we’re launching Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets in beta, and Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) becomes generally available as Claude Data. Whiteboards is a shared board where your team brainstorms with Claude, Sheets is a spreadsheet Claude builds and edits with you, and Claude Data adds data stories, certified queries, and live sharing. These are available on all paid plans.
Working with Claude on a project often meant moving the output over to another tool or program, where Claude didn’t have live access to follow progress and changes. Now, your documents, boards, sheets, and dashboards can stay in Claude, with access for your team to continue editing together. When ready, you can bring the outputs directly into tools from our partners and continue working there.
Claude Whiteboards
Many people use Claude as a thought partner, but brainstorming with it has typically meant copy-pasting the results elsewhere so you can then start brainstorming or collaborating with your coworkers. Now, you can talk through a messy plan out loud with Claude, and Claude can turn it into a board with a timeline with owners and dates, so you and your team can collaborate in real time. In a retro meeting, for example, everyone can add their notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft the action items for each person. You can focus on any part of the board by dragging a box around it and asking Claude questions. When you’re done brainstorming, Claude can turn the board into a doc or deck, or bring it into tools like Lucid, Miro, or Vani by Zoho, where you can continue working on it with your team.
Claude Sheets
Claude can now generate spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-downs, often from just a prompt like asking for a campaign tracker or a hiring budget. It can edit in the cells, outlining each new edit so you can track changes. You can share sheets with your team, so you and Claude can work on them together.
For now, sheets have simple spreadsheet functionality, but we are working on adding more. When you need the full functionality of Excel, you can export your file to .xlsx or CSV, or use Claude for Excel (opens in new tab). You can also continue working in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet.
Claude Data
Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) launched in beta in October, enabling teams to ask quick questions of their company’s data in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery, and ClickHouse. Starting today, it’s generally available as Claude Data. We changed the name because the way companies use their data is broader than dashboards, and the product now covers how they work more broadly. Certified queries and live sharing are in beta. Here are some ways teams can use Claude Data:
Create certified definitions of metrics. Your data team can certify the queries everyone should use, so you don’t end up building or working on dashboards with conflicting data. Charts built on these metrics carry a "certified" badge showing they’re certified.
Craft stories from data. You can work with Claude in Claude Data to draft data stories or narrated videos from your metrics, for you to review before sharing.
Share current numbers with everyone. With live sharing, your colleagues can see up-to-date numbers when they open a shared dashboard, even if they don’t have access to the connectors that keep that data current. Viewers see the results of the queries you’ve approved, and can’t run others with your access.
Match your look-and-feel. Design systems are now supported in Claude Data.
Get faster loading with caching. Previously, every dashboard would reload on every load. Now, dashboards support caching, and refresh cadences can be set on a per-dashboard…
